claims.text: Chemical disorder in a multi-principal-element high-entropy alloy produces local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions impede dislocation motion under dynamic loading.
Impeded dislocation motion increases the work-hardening rate.
The increased work-hardening rate delays plastic instability relative to a less chemically complex alloy.
The proposed initial material is a chemically disordered, single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Chemical complexity can be systematically varied from a disordered multi-element configuration to a reduced-component alloy while holding dynamic loading conditions constant.
The comparison is restricted to temperatures and strain rates at which dislocation glide operates.
Single-phase stability is maintained and secondary-phase formation is excluded during the comparison.
Randomly distributed atomic species create local lattice distortions.
Random lattice distortions act as dislocation-pinning points during dynamic deformation.
Distortion-mediated dislocation pinning contributes to a balance of high strength and ductility.
Greater chemical disorder will produce a higher work-hardening rate than reduced chemical complexity.
Greater chemical disorder will delay the onset of plastic instability relative to the reduced-component baseline.
Greater chemical disorder will enhance overall dynamic mechanical performance relative to the reduced-component baseline.
The proposed baseline is a less chemically complex, single-phase alloy subjected to the same dynamic conditions.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply when phase separation or elemental ordering occurs.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply at very high temperatures where diffusion dominates.
